name: Autologous fat transfer to face
lead: Autologous fat transfer to the face, also called facial fat grafting or lipofilling, is a surgical procedure in which a person's own fat is harvested from another part of the body, processed, and injected into the face to restore volume or alter contour. It is used for facial rejuvenation, where volume loss is recognised as a component of ageing, and for reconstructive and contouring purposes.[1][3][15]

Reviews describe the technique as having evolved from simple grafting to smaller-particle microfat and adipose-derived stem cell (nanofat) injection methods.[2] Plastic-surgery papers describe two long-standing concerns: that part of the transplanted fat is absorbed over time, and that lumps or bulges can form, particularly around the eyes.[3] Possible benefits beyond volume, such as improved skin texture, are also discussed by some surgeons.[3]

Unlike manufactured fillers, the material is the patient's own tissue, which proponents cite as an advantage; it requires a harvest site and is a surgical procedure, with associated risks. Wikipedia notes that embolic complications, including blindness, are more frequent with autologous fat than with hyaluronic acid fillers.[16] The procedure appears in appearance-modification discussion as an option for restoring hollow areas such as the cheeks, temples and under-eye region, and as a component of full-face contouring.

paras: Wikipedia describes fat grafting as having three stages: harvesting fat, typically by liposuction; processing it; and reinjecting it into the area to be improved, under general or local anaesthesia.[15] A paper on harvesting techniques notes that many facial plastic surgeons trained mainly in the head and neck region must work on other body areas to collect fat, and details approaches to lipoharvesting for facial transfer.[4]

Fat grafting is sometimes performed alone and sometimes combined with other procedures such as facelifts. A 2014 description of a lift-and-fill approach integrated restoration of individual facial fat compartments with repositioning of the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) during facelift surgery.[1] A 2023 retrospective study described rhinoplasty combined with simultaneous full-face fat transfer for balance of facial contour in Asian patients.[6]

Facial uses described in the literature include restoring volume lost with ageing, contouring, and treatment of the periorbital region.[1][3][15] Wikipedia notes that newer approaches to facial ageing restore volume using fat grafting, often combined with structural repositioning, because ageing involves fat atrophy, ligament laxity and descent of facial compartments.[15]

Registered studies include fat grafting in facial atrophy, craniofacial microsomia, post-burn facial scars and HIV-associated lipodystrophy, indicating use beyond purely cosmetic goals.[7][8][9][10][13]

Published literature is largely narrative reviews and surgeon-reported techniques rather than controlled trials. Review articles discuss microfat and nanofat grafting, long-term sequelae, and harvesting techniques.[2][3][4] A 2020 review covers autologous facial fat transfer as soft-tissue augmentation and regenerative therapy.[5]

Registered clinical studies include a phase 2 study of adipose-derived stem cells in facial fat grafting for facial atrophy (NCT02526576, 34 participants, completed), a phase 2 trial of fat grafts supplemented with adipose-derived regenerative cells in craniofacial microsomia (NCT01674439, 29 participants), a study of psychological morbidity and facial volume in HIV lipodystrophy (NCT01359917, 50 participants), and a small terminated study of concentrating stromal cells in fat grafts (NCT01564524).[7][8][9][10] Other registered studies examine facial skin quality after lipofilling (NCT07737639), a processing system (NCT05522426, not yet recruiting) and a device-assisted grafting technique (NCT06169670, 11 participants).[11][12][14]
A registered comparison of fat injection with platelet-rich plasma for post-burn facial scars (NCT04557514) also exists.[13]

A frequently cited limitation is that a share of the grafted fat is reabsorbed. Wikipedia reports that up to half may be reabsorbed in breast augmentation, and that weight gain or loss can alter results since transferred fat behaves like fat elsewhere in the body; survival is described as dependent on gentle handling and prompt reinjection.[15] Facial plastic-surgery authors discuss perceived absorption and dissipation as one of two main problems limiting wider acceptance.[3]
Proponents of microfat and nanofat techniques describe them as attempts to overcome early limitations, and some papers describe added skin-texture improvement.[2][3]

Wikipedia lists swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain or altered sensation, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities, injury from the cannula and fat necrosis as possible complications.[15] A review of limitations and long-term sequelae highlights lumps and bulges, particularly in the periorbital region.[3]

Retinal artery occlusion and blindness from retrograde embolization are rare but serious events described for facial fillers in general, and Wikipedia states that embolic complications are more frequent with autologous fat than with hyaluronic acid.[16]

timeline.event: Review of limitations, complications and long-term sequelae of facial fat transfer published.[3]
Lift-and-fill facelift integrating fat compartment restoration described.[1]
Review of microfat and nanofat techniques published.[2]
Retrospective study of rhinoplasty with full-face fat transfer in Asian patients published.[6]

card.summary: Using your own harvested fat as a face filler; well-established surgical technique, with variable retention and rare serious complications.
card.note: Part of the fat may be reabsorbed; rare vascular complications including vision loss are described.

quick.overview:
Facial fat transfer takes fat from elsewhere on your body and places it in the face to restore volume or change contour. Surgeons use it in facelifts, for hollow areas, and in reconstructive cases.

Most published material is narrative reviews and surgeon-reported technique, with some small registered trials of stem-cell enriched fat and processing devices.
quick.mechanism: Fat is collected by liposuction, processed, and injected as small amounts into target areas. Some of it survives as living tissue and some is absorbed; newer microfat and nanofat methods use finer preparations, partly for skin quality.
quick.risks: Reported problems include swelling, bruising, lumps or contour irregularities, donor-site issues and fat necrosis. Rare embolic events including blindness have been described, and Wikipedia reports these are more frequent with fat than with hyaluronic acid. Retention varies from person to person.
